p5.prefill-och-decode.2: Prefill runs the whole prompt at once. T rows are multiplied by the same weights, so every byte read from memory is used for many calculations. But prefill only becomes compute-bound once T is large enough: the break-even point is the same ratio that comes a few slides later, about 300 operations per byte read on an H100. A short prompt is memory-bound too.
p5.prefill-och-decode.3: Decode runs one token at a time. All 16 GB of weights are read to compute a single row. The GPU spends almost all its time waiting for memory (memory-bound).
p5.prefill-och-decode.4: Prefill decides how fast the first token arrives. Decode decides how fast the rest streams out. Almost everything an inference engine does is about getting decode to use the GPU better.
p5.prefill-och-decode.10: read W once, compute T rows
p5.kv-cache-steg-for-steg.2: K and V for a position never change once they have been computed (causal mask). So why recompute them?
p5.kv-cache-steg-for-steg.3: Without a cache, every decode step recomputes K and V for the whole sequence. With a cache, only the new position's K and V are computed and appended. The new token's query is then compared against all stored keys.
p5.kv-cache-steg-for-steg.4: The cache trades compute for memory: every token in every sequence occupies GPU memory in every layer for as long as the sequence lives.
p5.kv-cache-steg-for-steg.5: The figure shows one layer and one KV head. In reality the cache exists in all 32 layers and for all 8 KV heads.
p5.ett-decode-steg-med-shapes.3: No causal mask is needed in decode: the new token is last and gets to see everything.
p5.ett-decode-steg-med-shapes.4: The work in a decode step consists of two completely different parts:
p5.ett-decode-steg-med-shapes.5: Matmuls against weights (qkv, o, gate/up, down): the same cost regardless of context length. Shared across all sequences in a batch.
p5.ett-decode-steg-med-shapes.6: Attention against the cache: reads p+1 keys and values. Grows linearly with the context and is unique per sequence, so it cannot be shared.
p5.ett-decode-steg-med-shapes.7: That is why long conversations get more expensive per token: more and more of the time goes to reading the cache.
p5.hur-stor-blir-kv-cachen.1: How big is the KV cache?
p5.hur-stor-blir-kv-cachen.2:
bytes per token = 2 · L · n_kv · d_h · dtype
Llama-3-8B, bf16:
2 · 32 · 8 · 128 · 2 = 131 072 B = 128 KiB
p5.hur-stor-blir-kv-cachen.3: A conversation of 8000 tokens takes about 1.05 GB of cache. On an H100 with 80 GB and about 16 GB of weights, roughly 50 GB may remain for cache, around 390000 tokens across all sequences. The calculator shows memory arithmetic; context beyond 8192 requires, for example, Llama-3.1 rather than the original Llama-3-8B.
p5.hur-stor-blir-kv-cachen.4: This is the number that in practice decides how many users a GPU can serve at once.
p5.hur-stor-blir-kv-cachen.5: MLA (DeepSeek) caches a compressed latent vector instead of K and V: 576 numbers per token and layer.
p5.varfor-batching-raddar.2: An H100 reads about 3.35 TB/s and computes about 990 TFLOPS in bf16. The ratio is roughly 300: the GPU must do 300 operations per byte read to avoid waiting for memory.
p5.varfor-batching-raddar.3: Decode with one sequence does 2 operations per parameter and reads 2 bytes per parameter: a ratio of 1. The GPU sits idle 99% of the time.
p5.varfor-batching-raddar.4: With B sequences in the same step, the weights are read once but used B times. Throughput grows almost linearly until the compute or the KV memory runs out.
p5.varfor-batching-raddar.5: Idealized model for Llama-3-8B in bf16 on an H100. Real numbers are lower, but the shape holds.
p5.latensmatt.1: Latency metrics: TTFT, ITL and throughput
p5.latensmatt.7: TTFT (time to first token): queue time plus prefill. Grows with the prompt length and with how much else is running.
p5.latensmatt.8: ITL / TPOT (inter-token latency, time per output token): the time for one decode step. This is what the user experiences as writing speed.
p5.latensmatt.9: Throughput: tokens per second summed over all users. A bigger batch raises throughput but also the ITL for each of them.
p5.latensmatt.10: A server always picks a point on the curve between fast for one and efficient for many. vLLM's scheduler parameters are the knobs for that.
p5.kvantisering.2: Fewer bits per weight means fewer bytes to read per decode step and room for more KV cache.
p5.kvantisering.3: Weight-only int4 (AWQ, GPTQ): weights are stored with 4 bits plus one scale factor per group of, say, 128 weights. The kernel unpacks to bf16 on the fly. Good for memory-bound decode.
p5.kvantisering.4: FP8 (W8A8): both weights and activations in 8 bits. On an H100 the tensor cores compute twice as fast in FP8, so prefill gets faster too.
p5.kvantisering.5: FP8 KV cache: halves the cache, which means twice as many tokens in memory.
p5.kvantisering.6: The price is a little precision. Int4 has only 16 levels per group, so the scale factor has to be chosen wisely.
p5.testa-dig-sjalv-inferens.1: Test yourself: inference and the KV cache
p5.testa-dig-sjalv-inferens.2: How big is the KV cache for 16 concurrent sequences of 4,000 tokens in Llama-3-8B with bf16?
p5.testa-dig-sjalv-inferens.4: Why doesn't decode become twice as slow when the batch goes from 1 to 2 sequences?
p5.testa-dig-sjalv-inferens.5: The step is dominated by reading the weights, and that happens once regardless of batch size. The extra computation and KV reads for the second sequence are small in comparison.
p5.testa-dig-sjalv-inferens.6: What does a long system prompt affect most: TTFT or ITL?
p5.testa-dig-sjalv-inferens.7: Mainly TTFT, since it has to be prefilled. ITL also rises slightly because every decode step reads more cached positions. A prefix-cache hit can avoid the shared prefix’s prefill work; queueing and the uncached suffix still contribute to TTFT.
p5.testa-dig-sjalv-inferens.8: Why do int4 weights help decode more than prefill?
p5.testa-dig-sjalv-inferens.9: Weight-only int4 reduces the weight bytes by about 4 compared with bf16. That can help bandwidth-bound decode, but KV reads, unpacking, kernels and batching limit the latency gain. Long-prompt prefill often spends more time on arithmetic. Neither phase has a universal speedup guarantee.
